common_name: Haokea Taro (Hawaiian Upland White-Fleshed Poi Taro)

planting.note: Set huli (corm-top cuttings) once soil has warmed; unlike many wetland poi taros, Haokea is traditionally a dryland (upland) cultivar and performs well in consistently moist but not flooded upland beds.

directions: Haokea is a long-documented Hawaiian upland taro variety, recorded among the dozens of named kalo cultivars catalogued by early 20th-century Hawaii Agricultural Experiment Station taro surveys, and still maintained today by Hawaiian cultural-agriculture programs. It is grown as a dryland crop in evenly moist, well-drained upland mo'o (rows) rather than flooded lo'i, and is especially valued for its very pale, near-white corm flesh, which cooks down into a light-colored poi distinct from the purplish poi of Lehua-type taros. Give it rich, consistently damp soil, partial shade from the harshest afternoon sun, and steady fertility, since upland taro lacks the buffering that flooded water gives wetland types. Corms and leaves must be thoroughly cooked to break down calcium oxalate crystals before eating.
sources: University of Hawaii CTAHR, Taro Varieties in Hawaii
Whitney, Bowers & Takahashi, 'Taro Varieties in Hawaii,' Hawaii Agricultural Experiment Station Bulletin 84
Ho'oulu ka 'Ulu / Hawaii taro variety identification guides

planting.note: Plant container-grown or tissue-cultured trees in spring in rich, deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Ma'afala is prized among breadfruit varieties for its compact, dwarf growth habit and unusually early, heavy fruiting compared to taller seeded types.

directions: Ma'afala originated in Samoa and is one of the most widely propagated named breadfruit varieties in the Pacific, selected and distributed through the Breadfruit Institute's germplasm collection in Hawaii because of its small stature, early bearing age, and heavy, reliable seedless fruit set. Compared to tall, slow-to-fruit Hawaiian seedling ulu, Ma'afala trees begin producing within two to four years and stay compact enough for home gardens and agroforestry plantings. The medium, round-to-oval fruit has pale yellow-green skin and starchy, slightly sweet flesh that is traditionally roasted, steamed, or fermented, and it has become a cornerstone variety in Pacific and Hawaiian ulu orchards as well as international breadfruit-for-food-security programs. Give it deep, fertile, well-drained soil, consistent moisture, and full sun, and protect young trees from wind and any cold below the mid-50s F.
sources: Breadfruit Institute, National Tropical Botanical Garden
Ragone, D. 'Breadfruit Varieties in the Pacific' (Artocarpus altilis germplasm collection)
University of Hawaii CTAHR, 'Ulu (Breadfruit)' fact sheet

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Shalakh needs the hot, dry, continental summers of its native Ararat Valley to fully develop its sugar content, and a sheltered site helps protect its early bloom from spring frost.

directions: Shalakh is one of the oldest named apricot landraces of Armenia's Ararat Valley, a region long credited as part of the apricot's center of diversity, and it remains a benchmark variety in Armenian pomological collections and home orchards. The medium to large fruit has golden-orange skin, often with a faint pink blush, and notably sweet, firm flesh with a high sugar content that makes it especially prized for drying into Armenian dried apricots (choreg) and for distilling into apricot brandy. Trees bloom early, so a sheltered site away from late spring frost pockets is important, and they perform best with the hot, dry summers and cold winters typical of continental growing regions. Shalakh has also served as breeding stock for many modern Armenian and Soviet-era apricot cultivars seeking its intense sweetness and freestone character.
sources: Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) apricot genetic resources reports, Armenia
Armenian National Academy of Sciences, Institute of Botany fruit germplasm collections
International Society for Horticultural Science (ISHS) Acta Horticulturae, Armenian apricot germplasm studies

common_name: Lapin Puikula Potato (Finnish Lapland Heirloom Potato)

planting.note: Plant certified seed tubers in cool, fertile, well-drained soil once the ground is workable; Lapin Puikula is a long-season landrace that depends on the nearly round-the-clock summer daylight of the far north to bulk up its elongated tubers.

directions: Lapin Puikula ('Lapland fingerling') is a traditional Finnish landrace potato grown for generations in Finnish Lapland and recognized since 1997 with EU Protected Designation of Origin status as a distinct regional product. Its curved, elongated tubers have yellow skin and deep yellow, notably sweet-flavored flesh, a trait attributed to the long, cool, nearly continuous daylight of the subarctic growing season that slows starch-to-sugar conversion. It is a late-maturing variety that needs the full length of the short northern summer, and growers outside subarctic latitudes should expect somewhat different flavor and sizing. Harvest once foliage dies back in fall and cure tubers in a cool, dark, well-ventilated space before long-term storage.
sources: European Commission eAmbrosia PDO/PGI register (Lapin Puikula)
ProAgria Lapland potato growers' association
Nordic Genetic Resource Center (NordGen) potato landrace documentation

planting.note: Plant certified seed tubers in cool, loose, fertile soil as soon as it can be worked; Mandel sets many small, knobby tubers per plant, so hill soil generously as stems grow to maximize usable yield.

directions: Mandel, known in Sweden as mandelpotatis, is an old fingerling landrace long cultivated in the tills and silt soils of Dalarna and other inland Swedish regions, prized for its dense, nutty-flavored, waxy yellow flesh. Plants produce clusters of small, elongated, knobby tubers with pale tan skin, yielding less by weight than modern round potatoes but valued highly for flavor and for holding together in traditional dishes. It has been documented and maintained by Swedish heritage-crop preservation programs (POM) as part of the country's traditional kitchen-garden potato diversity, and is sold in North America under names such as Swedish Peanut Fingerling. Grow in full sun with consistent moisture during tuber set, and harvest once vines die back in fall for a dense, long-storing crop.
sources: Swedish Programme for Diversity of Cultivated Plants (POM)
NordGen (Nordic Genetic Resource Center) potato landrace archive
Seed Savers Exchange heirloom potato collection notes

planting.note: Direct sow in early to midsummer so roots bulk up in cool autumn weather; Bangholm is the classic Swedish-bred swede that stands behind many modern commercial purple-top rutabaga strains.

directions: Bangholm is a historic Swedish rutabaga type, selected from the Scandinavian swede landraces that form the base of modern purple-top rutabagas grown across Europe and North America today. Roots are round to slightly oblong with a purple-tinged crown fading to pale yellow below, enclosing firm, fine-grained, pale orange flesh with the mellow, sweet flavor typical of well-grown Nordic swedes. Direct sow into deep, fertile, well-drained soil and thin seedlings to a hand's width apart, since crowded roots stay small and misshapen. Leave roots in the ground through a light frost or two before harvest, as cold weather measurably sweetens the flavor, and store in cool, humid conditions for winter keeping.
sources: NordGen (Nordic Genetic Resource Center) brassica landrace archive
Swedish Board of Agriculture heritage vegetable records
Royal Horticultural Society, swede/rutabaga cultivar history

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, with a compatible pollinizer nearby; Åkerö is well adapted to short, cool Nordic growing seasons.

directions: Åkerö is one of Sweden's oldest and most widely grown heirloom apples, first recorded in the 18th century at the Åkerö estate in Södermanland and carried for generations across Scandinavian home orchards. The medium-sized fruit has greenish-yellow skin heavily flushed and striped with red, and crisp, juicy, aromatic flesh balancing sweetness with a light tartness that suits both fresh eating and traditional Swedish baking. It ripens in autumn and stores notably well into winter for an apple of its age, a trait that made it a dependable keeper in the era before refrigeration. Åkerö remains a benchmark variety in Swedish pomological collections (POM) and heritage orchards, valued for reliable cropping and hardiness under short, cool Nordic summers.
sources: Swedish Programme for Diversity of Cultivated Plants (POM)
Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences (SLU) pomological collections
NordGen (Nordic Genetic Resource Center) fruit tree archive
